'''Nordmann's greenshank''' ('''''Tringa guttifer''''') or the '''spotted greenshank''' is a [[wader]] in the large family Scolopacidae, the typical waders. They are considered endangered by the [[IUCN Red List|International Union for Conservation of Nature]] (IUCN) Red List and are typically found within the [[East Asian–Australasian Flyway|East Asian-Australasian Flyway]].

==Description==
Nordmann's greenshank is a medium-sized [[sandpiper]], at 29–32 cm (11–13 in) long, with a slightly upturned, bicoloured [[Beak|bill]], and relatively short yellow legs<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maleko |first=Philipp N. |last2=Pronkevich |first2=Vladimir V. |last3=Maslovsky |first3=Konstantin S. |date=2021 |title=Nordmann's Greenshank (Tringa guttifer), version 2.0 |url=https://birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/norgre1/cur/introduction |journal=Birds of the World |language=en |doi=10.2173/bow.norgre1.02 |issn=2771-3105|url-access=subscription }}</ref>. Breeding adults have darker plumage than their non-breeding counterparts. These adults often appear boldly marked, with dark brown spangling on their back, chest, and head and a white underbelly.They have a heavily streaked head and upper neck; broad, blackish, crescentic spots on lower neck and breast; and darker lores. Breeding adult bills are darker and less obviously bicolored as well. Non-breeding adults have a lighter brown to gray plumage along their back and minimal spotting along their neck and chest. Their bills are light nearest the head and dark as it extends to the tip. Chicks are light brown with mottled black and dark brown stripes across their back and head. Similar to the North American [[Blue jay]], the Nordmann's greenshank eggs are a pale blue-green with darker gray to brown speckling that condenses near the widest end of the egg. 
[[File:TotanusHaughtoniSmit.jpg|thumb|upright|left]]

==Distribution==
Nordmann's greenshank is found primarily within the [[East Asian–Australasian Flyway|East Asian-Australasian Flyway]] and as of 2023, the wild population ranges from 1500 to 2000 individuals<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cao |first=Ranxing |last2=Liang |first2=Waner |last3=Guo |first3=Jia |last4=Yang |first4=Hongyan |last5=Sun |first5=Lili |last6=Chen |first6=Qing |last7=Yu |first7=Tao |last8=Ren |first8=Sicheng |last9=Lu |first9=Cai |last10=Lei |first10=Guangchun |last11=Jia |first11=Yifei |date=2023-01-01 |title=Global population estimate and conservation gap analysis for the Nordmann's Greenshank (Tringa guttifer) |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2053716623000257 |journal=Avian Research |volume=14 |article-number=100099 |doi=10.1016/j.avrs.2023.100099 |issn=2053-7166|doi-access=free }}</ref>. Breeding populations are found in eastern [[Russia]] along the south-western and northern coasts of the [[Sea of Okhotsk]] and on [[Sakhalin Island]]. Their non-breeding range is not fully defined, but significant numbers have been recorded in [[South Korea]], mainland [[China]], [[Hong Kong]], [[Taiwan]] during the migratory season. During winter, these birds can be found in [[Bangladesh]], [[Thailand]], [[Cambodia]], [[Vietnam]] and Peninsular [[Malaysia]]. They have also been recorded on passage or during winter in [[Japan]], [[North Korea]], [[India]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[Myanmar]], [[Singapore]], the [[Philippines]] and [[Indonesia]]. There are unconfirmed records from [[Nepal]] and [[Guam]] (to the U.S.).. They have been recorded several times on [[Eighty Mile Beach]] in Western Australia. Recently, an individual was discovered on Cairns Esplanade in Queensland, Australia. This individual was known to have over-wintered there from December 2020 to May 2021. In mid-December 2021 what is thought to be the same individual bird, returned to Cairns Esplanade. It has now returned for four straight seasons, being regularly seen in 2022 and 2023.

== Nesting ==
Nordmann's Greenshank has been shown to have a nesting preference towards partially dried boglands containing stands of larch trees. Their nests are found in three primary locations among these habitats: 1) arboreal nests on larch branches, 2) ground nests at the base of sapling larch trees, and 3) ground nests at the base of mature larch trees<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Maslovsky |first=Konstantin S. |last2=Maleko |first2=Philipp N. |last3=Pronkevich |first3=Vladimir V. |last4=Slaght |first4=Jonathan C. |last5=Powell |first5=Abby N. |date=2023 |title=First nests of Endangered Nordmann's Greenshank Tringa guttifer found in over 40 years indicate nesting plasticity |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S095927092200051X/type/journal_article |journal=Bird Conservation International |language=en |volume=33 |doi=10.1017/S095927092200051X |issn=0959-2709|url-access=subscription }}</ref>. Nests are constructed with small twigs from these larches and lined with lichens and other soft foliage. Such composition includes [[Pinus pumila|dwarf Siberian pine]] (''Pinus pumila)'' needles, [[Bryoria fuscescens|speckled horsehair]] (''Bryoria fuscescens''), [[Melanohalea olivacea|melanelia]] (''Melanohalea olivacea''), [[Rim lichen|rim]] (''Lecanora symmicta''), [[Evernia mesomorpha|ring]] (''Evernia mesomorpha''), [[Hypogymnia|tube]] (''Hypogymnia sachalinensis''), [[Cladonia arbuscula|Bering reindeer]] (''Cladonia cf. arbuscula''), and [[Usnea|bearded]] (''Usnea'' sp.)<ref name=":0" />. Ring, tube, and Bering reindeer lichens are light in color, behaviorally used to camouflage their eggs. Clutches typically contain 3-4 eggs.

== Molting Patterns ==
Molting season for the Nordmann's greenshank occurs in late summer and early fall during the months of July through October. Molting occurs during their migration south during the non-breeding season. Molting behavior lasts on average 65 days and the birds typically halt migration while molting<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Ziyou |last2=Lagassé |first2=Benjamin J. |last3=Xiao |first3=Hui |last4=Jackson |first4=Micha V. |last5=Chiang |first5=Chung-Yu |last6=Melville |first6=David S. |last7=Leung |first7=Kar Sin Katherine |last8=Li |first8=Jing |last9=Zhang |first9=Lin |last10=Peng |first10=He-Bo |last11=Gan |first11=Xiaojing |last12=Liu |first12=Wen-Liang |last13=Ma |first13=Zhijun |last14=Choi |first14=Chi-Yeung |date=2020-05-08 |title=The southern Jiangsu coast is a critical moulting site for Spoon-billed Sandpiper Calidris pygmaea and Nordmann's Greenshank Tringa guttifer |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0959270920000210/type/journal_article |journal=Bird Conservation International |language=en |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=649–660 |doi=10.1017/S0959270920000210 |issn=0959-2709|via=Cambridge University Direct|hdl=11370/76a7233a-004d-4569-8660-89b2ce5f7c4c |hdl-access=free }}</ref>.

== Roosting Behavior ==
During the non-breeding season in the Inner Gulf of Thailand, the Nordmann's greenshank has been shown to have roost preferences determined by tide cycles. Birds will choose artificial roosting areas such as saltpans and aquaculture farms during oceanic high tides, but tend to prefer mudflats along the coastline. Roost sites are chosen based on the characteristics: 1) depth of water in selected sites, 2) travel distance for foraging sites, 3) human disturbance risk, and 4) competition with other shorebirds<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yu |first=Chenxing |last2=Ngoprasert |first2=Dusit |last3=Round |first3=Philip D. |last4=Pierce |first4=Andrew J. |last5=Savini |first5=Tommaso |last6=Gale |first6=George A. |date=2019-03-27 |title=Roost selection of the endangered Spotted Greenshank (Tringa guttifer) in critical habitat in the Inner Gulf of Thailand |journal=Avian Research |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |page=9 |doi=10.1186/s40657-019-0148-7  |doi-access=free|issn=2053-7166|publication-date=2020-05-08}}</ref>. 

==Taxonomy==
Before being classified as the genus ''Tringa,'' the Nordmann's greenshank was formerly placed in the [[Monotypic taxon|monotypic]] genus ''Pseudototanus''. A full mitochondrial DNA reference genome was published in 2019<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Liu |first=Wei |last2=He |first2=Yuxiao |last3=Ding |first3=Jingjing |last4=Chang |first4=Qing |date=2019-07-03 |title=The complete mitochondrial genome of the Spotted Greenshank Tringa guttifer (Charadriiforemes: Charadriidae) |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/23802359.2019.1629349 |journal=Mitochondrial DNA Part B |language=en |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=2353–2354 |doi=10.1080/23802359.2019.1629349 |issn=2380-2359 |pmc=7687452 |pmid=33365540}}</ref>. This DNA places these birds firmly within the ''Tringa'' genus, with the closest phylogenetic relative being the [[willet]] (''Tringa semipalmata'').  

[[File:Common Greenshank & Nordmann's Greenshank, Cairns, Australia.jpg|thumb|Common greenshank and Nordmann's greenshank, Cairns, Australia]]
[[File:Nordmann's Greenshank Cairns Australia.jpg|thumb|Nordmann's greenshank, Cairns, Australia]]

== Conservation ==
''Tringa guttifer'' was placed on the IUCN Red List in 1988 as a "Threatened" species, and was moved to the "Endangered" category in 1994<ref>{{Cite journal |last=BirdLife International (BirdLife International) |date=2024-07-15 |title=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species: Tringa guttifer |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22693225/223484923 |journal=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250429081820/https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22693225/223484923 |archive-date=2025-04-29}}</ref>. This classification remains into 2026. 

Currently, there is no official conservation strategy being used for this species. The primary threats to ''T. guttifer'' are habitat loss, disturbance, and illegal netting by humans<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maleko |first=Philipp N. |last2=Sinhaseni |first2=Khwankhao |last3=Khamaye |first3=Jirut |last4=Pichayamahoot |first4=Porames |last5=Round |first5=Philip D. |last6=Allen |first6=Desmond |last7=Robards |first7=Martin |last8=Slaght |first8=Jonathan C. |date=2025-01-15 |title=Threats to shorebirds, particularly Spotted Greenshank Tringa guttifer, along the Inner Gulf of Thailand |url=https://www.waderstudygroup.org/article/18653/ |journal=Wader Study |volume=131 |issue=3 |doi=10.18194/ws.00354|url-access=subscription }}</ref>.
